sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Grand Rapids?
sections.html:
The City of Grand Rapids Treasurer's Office bills and collects property tax on city parcels, and the City Assessor sets the values the bill is built on. Grand Rapids sits in Kent County, so the county shows up on the winter bill and again if a bill goes delinquent.

The city treasurer's office is on the second floor of City Hall at 300 Monroe Ave NW, Suite 220, and takes calls at 616-456-3020. Assessment questions go to the assessor's line at 616-456-3081. Bills can also be searched and paid online through the city's BS&A Online portal, which needs no account.

Grand Rapids is the second most populated city in Michigan, with 201,183 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate and a land area of about 44.8 square miles. The city grew up around a set of rapids on the Grand River, and a mailing address carries a quadrant letter code (NE, NW, SE or SW) split at Fulton Street and Division Avenue. The city counts 37 neighborhoods, from Heritage Hill and Eastown to Garfield Park and Alger Heights, and the tax bill for each one follows the same rules.

sections.h2: When are Grand Rapids property taxes due?
sections.html:
Summer bills are due July 31 and winter bills are due February 14. If either date lands on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day, and the due date is printed on the bill.

The two bills carry different charges. The summer bill is the larger one and holds the City, Kent Intermediate School District, Grand Rapids Community College and State of Michigan levies, plus the State Education Tax. The winter bill carries only county charges, with rates approved by the Kent County Board of Commissioners.

A bill that never arrives is still owed. Call the treasurer at 616-456-3020 and a duplicate will be sent. Late payments are not reported to the credit bureaus, according to the city's policy page, though the fees themselves are real.

sections.h2: How is a Grand Rapids tax bill calculated?
sections.html:
The bill starts with taxable value, which is the figure the city uses for tax, and it can sit at or below the assessed value. The assessor looks at market value every year to set both numbers.

  • Principal Residence Exemption (PRE): removes 18 school operating mills for owner-occupied homes, in whole or in part for a duplex or a home with rented rooms.
  • Millage rate: mills multiplied by each $1,000 of taxable value, with the full rate depending on the school district the home sits in.
  • Property Tax Administration Fee: a 1% fee added to the total.
  • Estimator: the city offers an online tool that takes the school district, taxable value and PRE percentage.

The city's own worked example uses a $50,000 taxable value with full PRE in the Grand Rapids school district and arrives at $1,729.07 for the summer and winter bills combined. That example used the 2017 millage rate, so treat it as a demonstration of the formula and pull the current rate from the Kent County website.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Grand Rapids assessment?
sections.html:
File a petition with the City Assessor during the Assessor's Review held each February, then appeal that decision to the March Board of Review by letter or by appointment. The March board only hears owners who first went to the assessor.

The July and December Boards of Review work on a narrower list. They can act on qualified errors the assessor verifies, such as a clerical mistake, a mutual mistake of fact or a measurement error, for the current year and one prior year. They may also grant a poverty exemption for the current year only. The statute behind these boards is MCL 211.53b.

A Board of Review decision does not pause the bill. If the board changes the amount, the treasurer adjusts the bill within 30 days of receiving the final report, and the original bill stays due on its date or the late fees apply. Refunds go to whoever paid the tax.

sections.h2: What relief programs exist for Grand Rapids homeowners?
sections.html:
A household can ask the treasurer to push the summer due date to the winter due date. The city's deferment requires household income under $40,000, that the home is a principal residence, and that the owner is one of the following:

  • A senior citizen over 62
  • Paraplegic or quadriplegic
  • Totally and permanently disabled
  • Blind
  • An eligible veteran, service member, or the widow or widower of one

The city usually approves these requests and only calls when it needs more information. The application is online, as a printable PDF, or in person at the treasurer's office. Separate exemptions exist for disabled veterans and for owners in poverty, and the city's Property Tax Payments and Policies page links the instructions.

Owners who cannot pay in full can ask about installment payments, which carry a penalty. Renaissance zone residents can qualify for certain tax exemptions each year, but never if a property tax payment anywhere in Michigan was ever late.

sections.h2: How do I claim the principal residence exemption in Grand Rapids?
sections.html:
File the PRE affidavit with the City Assessor by June 1. MCL 211.7cc requires that the owner qualifies under the statute, lives in the property as a principal residence, and has no disqualifying factor.

A missed deadline is not always final. The assessor may ask for proof that the home was owner occupied on June 1 and can then correct the current year and up to three prior years.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Grand Rapids taxes and a sale?
sections.html:
On March 1, any unpaid real property bill, summer or winter, moves from the city to the Kent County Treasurer. The county adds its own late fees, and Kent County's treasurer page describes a 4% administrative fee and the county's authority to sell parcels that are more than 24 months delinquent after a court order. Delinquent personal property and most abatement bills stay with the city.

Taxes affect a sale in two places. A warranty deed recorded in Michigan needs a county treasurer certificate under MCL 211.135, which covers whether taxes were paid for the five years before the deed. And the title company will ask for a payoff figure on any balance, so request one from the city treasurer for current bills or from the Kent County Treasurer for anything past March 1.

Homeowners in this spot have options: sell on the open market, sell as-is to a cash buyer, or pay the balance first. Whichever route fits, get written payoff numbers before you set a closing date.

faqs.q: When is the Grand Rapids summer tax bill due?
faqs.a: July 31, or the next business day if that falls on a weekend. Bills are mailed the first week of July, and a 1% charge applies for each month the balance stays unpaid.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Grand Rapids property tax after March 1?
faqs.a: The Kent County Treasurer. On March 1 unpaid real property bills leave the city treasurer, and the county adds its own late fees and an administration fee.

faqs.q: Can I get more time to pay my summer bill in Grand Rapids?
faqs.a: Possibly. A household earning under $40,000 that lives in the home can apply for deferment to the winter due date if the owner is over 62, disabled, blind, or an eligible veteran or surviving spouse. Installment plans with a penalty are also available through the treasurer.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to claim the principal residence exemption in Grand Rapids?
faqs.a: June 1, filed with the City Assessor. If it is missed, the assessor may accept proof of owner occupancy as of that date and adjust the current year and up to three prior years.

faqs.q: Does a Board of Review appeal stop my Grand Rapids tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The original bill remains due on its date. If the board changes your value, the treasurer revises the bill within 30 days of the board's final report and refunds go to the party that paid.
